name: Ruby
card_line: A back-office agent that logs hours, drafts invoices, and tracks payments.
built_with: Python, SQLite, DeepSeek via OpenRouter, Claude Code, Gemini
time_to_build: Five days of building (November 16-20, 2026), after a week of planning

snapshot.problem: Freelance billing ran on manual entry and copy-paste, which caused math errors and missed invoice follow-ups.
snapshot.what_i_built: An agent she chats with. It logs hours, nudges her to act, drafts invoice emails, and asks before anything important.
snapshot.result: Invoices go out the same way every week, and unpaid ones get flagged. I expect it to save about an hour a week.

problem: The designer ran all of her admin by hand in a spreadsheet. Hours were typed into cells, totals were worked out by hand, and every invoice was built and emailed manually. It was a copy-paste nightmare that led to miscalculations. Following up on unpaid invoices depended on remembering to check, so it got missed. Her main client also caps weekly hours, so she had to keep a running total.

how_it_works.text: She tells Ruby what she worked on in a plain sentence, like "2.5 hours on the holiday mailer today."
The model turns the sentence into a date, hours, and an item. If something is missing, it asks instead of guessing.
Code applies the billing rules, catches likely duplicates, saves the entry, and warns her as she nears her weekly hours cap.
Ruby nudges her at the end of any workday with nothing logged, and flags every invoice that's past due.
At the end of the week, Ruby builds the invoice PDF in her own layout and drafts the email to the client.
She reviews the preview and says yes. Ruby saves the draft in Gmail, and she hits Send herself.
She confirms each payment Ruby matched from her inbox. Ruby marks the invoice paid and reminds her what to set aside for taxes.

decisions.decision: A person owns the final mile.
decisions.reason: Ruby does the prep. She confirms every payment match and sends every invoice and email herself. Ruby's email connection can't send, and code holds changes until she says yes.

decisions.decision: I watched how she actually invoiced before writing any code.
decisions.reason: That turned up a step I hadn't planned for: her client's processor emails a confirmation, so Ruby can tell "sent" from "received" without asking.

decisions.decision: The model handles language, and code handles money.
decisions.reason: The model only turns sentences into fields. Rounding, billing math, the hours cap, and the no-delete rule run in code and the database.

decisions.decision: No bank login, and no AI on payment emails.
decisions.reason: Ruby matches payments from read-only email alerts, checks they really came from the bank and the client, and keeps that text away from the model.

decisions.decision: Ruby is polite, and it sticks to business.
decisions.reason: Its instructions give it one job and only the tools for that job, so a conversation that drifts gets steered back to the work.

results.label: End-to-end test chats logged correctly, checked against what was saved (22 of 26 before I fixed what the first run caught)
Past invoices rebuilt from her records with matching totals. The check caught a rate change the spec had missed.

next: Draft a follow-up email when an invoice goes past due, so she only has to review it and hit Send.
Track her admin time for a month and replace my one-hour estimate. I should have timed the old process before I started.
Keep the model test chats in the project and rerun them after every change. Right now only the code tests rerun automatically.
